extracted.intended_audience: editors, publishers, journalists and external contributors at publications regulated by IPSO (UK press organisations)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements for editorial conduct, content and procedures that editors/publishers regulated by IPSO must follow for print and online publications, including when public interest exceptions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble — purpose and balance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Code sets the framework for highest professional standards balancing individual rights and the public’s right to know; it should be honoured to the letter and spirit and interpreted neither so narrowly as to compromise individual rights nor so broadly as to infringe freedom of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the Code is cornerstone of voluntary self-regulation; allows permissible press activities (inform, be partisan, challenge, shock, satirise, entertain) and should not prevent publication in the public interest. Emphasises balance between privacy/individual rights and freedom of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application & enforcement; complaints handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and publishers are responsible for applying the Code to editorial material in both printed and online versions and for ensuring staff and external contributors observe it; the Code is enforced by IPSO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must maintain in-house procedures to resolve complaints swiftly and cooperate with IPSO where required. A publication subject to an adverse adjudication must publish it in full and with due prominence as required by IPSO. The Code is written/reviewed by the Editors' Code Committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Press must take care not to publish inaccurate, misleading or distorted information or images, including headlines not supported by the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: i) Avoid inaccuracies, misleading or distorted information/images and unsupported headlines. ii) Significant inaccuracies, misleading statements or distortions must be corrected promptly and with due prominence and an apology published where appropriate; prominence as required by IPSO in cases involving the regulator. iii) Give a fair opportunity to reply to significant inaccuracies when reasonably called for. iv) Distinguish clearly between comment, conjecture and fact. v) Report fairly and accurately the outcome of a defamation action unless settlement/agreed statement says otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone is entitled to respect for their private and family life, home, physical and mental health, and correspondence, including digital communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must justify intrusions into private life without consent; take account of complainant’s own public disclosures and whether material is in or will become public domain. It is unacceptable to photograph individuals without consent in places where there is a reasonable expectation of privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must not engage in intimidation, harassment or persistent pursuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not persist in questioning, telephoning, pursuing or photographing individuals once asked to desist; do not remain on property when asked to leave or follow them. If requested, journalists must identify themselves and whom they represent. Editors must enforce these principles and avoid using non-compliant material from other sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrusion into grief or shock
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases involving personal grief or shock, enquiries and approaches must be made with sympathy and discretion and publication handled sensitively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions should not restrict the right to report legal proceedings. Approach victims and bereaved persons with care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting suicide
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting suicide, care should be taken to avoid excessive detail of the method used to prevent simulative acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance between preventing imitation and the media’s right to report legal proceedings; avoid excessive methodological detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children — general protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Protective rules for pupils and children under 16 regarding approach, photography, interviews and payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: i) Pupils should be free to complete their time at school without unnecessary intrusion. ii) Do not approach or photograph at school without permission of school authorities. iii) Children under 16 must not be interviewed or photographed on welfare issues unless an adult with legal parental responsibility or similarly responsible adult consents. iv) Children under 16 must not be paid for material involving their welfare, nor parents/guardians paid for material about their children, unless clearly in the child’s interest. v) Do not use a parent's fame/notoriety as sole justification for publishing details of a child's private life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children in sex cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The press must not, even if legally free to do so, identify children under 16 who are victims or witnesses in cases involving sex offences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In any press report of a sexual offence involving a child: i) Do not identify the child. ii) The adult may be identified. iii) Do not use the word 'incest' where a child victim might be identified. iv) Take care that nothing implies the relationship between the accused and the child.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hospitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must identify themselves and obtain permission from a responsible executive before entering non-public areas of hospitals or similar institutions to pursue enquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrictions on intruding into privacy are particularly relevant to enquiries about individuals in hospitals or similar institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Constraints and considerations when identifying relatives/friends of accused/convicted persons and naming minors in relation to criminal matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: i) Relatives or friends of persons convicted or accused should not generally be identified without consent unless genuinely relevant. ii) Pay particular regard to vulnerable children under 18 who witness or are victims of crime; this should not restrict reporting legal proceedings. iii) Generally avoid naming children under 18 after arrest but before youth court appearance unless name already public or consent given (does not restrict naming juveniles in crown court or where anonymity is lifted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clandestine devices and subterfuge
rubrics_metrics.description: The press must not seek to obtain or publish material acquired by hidden cameras, clandestine listening devices, intercepting communications, unauthorised removal of documents/photos, or accessing digitally-held information without consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engaging in misrepresentation or subterfuge (including via agents) can generally be justified only in the public interest and only when the material cannot be obtained by other means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Victims of sexual assault
rubrics_metrics.description: The press must not identify or publish material likely to lead to identification of a victim of sexual assault unless there is adequate justification and they are legally free to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists may make enquiries but must take care and exercise discretion to avoid unjustified disclosure of identity; ensure adequate justification/legal freedom before publishing identifying material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: The press must avoid prejudicial or pejorative reference to an individual's race, colour, religion, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation or to any physical or mental illness or disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details of an individual’s race, colour, religion, gender identity, sexual orientation, physical or mental illness or disability must be avoided unless genuinely relevant to the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules governing use of financial information and conflicts of interest when reporting on shares and securities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: i) Do not use for personal profit financial information received in advance of general publication, nor pass it to others. ii) Disclose significant financial interests to the editor/financial editor if writing about shares/securities where you/close family have a significant interest. iii) Do not buy or sell shares/securities about which you have written recently or intend to write in near future, either directly or via nominees/agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists have a moral obligation to protect confidential sources of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect sources unless there is an overriding and justifiable reason not to; this is a moral obligation underpinning investigative journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness payments in criminal trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrictions on payments to witnesses or persons likely to be called once proceedings are active and guidance where proceedings are not yet active but foreseeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: i) No payment/offer of payment to a witness (or person likely to be called) once proceedings are active as defined by the Contempt of Court Act 1981; prohibition lasts until certain case-ending events occur. ii) Where proceedings are not yet active but likely/foreseeable, editors must not make or offer payment unless publication is demonstrably in the public interest and there is an overriding need to pay; reasonable steps must be taken to ensure payments do not influence evidence; payments must never be conditional on trial outcome. iii) Any payment/offer made to a person later cited to give evidence must be disclosed to prosecution and defence and the witness advised of this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment to criminals
rubrics_metrics.description: Payments for stories, pictures or information that seek to exploit or glamorise crime must not be made to convicted/confessed criminals or their associates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: i) Do not make payments directly or via agents to convicted/confessed criminals or associates (including family/friends/colleagues) if it seeks to exploit or glorify crime. ii) Editors invoking public interest to justify payment must demonstrate good reason to believe public interest is served; if no public interest emerges, material should not be published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest exceptions and test
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be exceptions to clauses marked * where they can be demonstrated to be in the public interest; editors invoking the public interest must demonstrate reasonable belief that publication would serve and be proportionate to the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Public interest includes (but not confined to): detecting/exposing crime or serious impropriety; protecting public health/safety; protecting public from being misled; disclosing failure to comply with obligations; disclosing miscarriage of justice; raising/contributing to public debate about serious impropriety/unethical conduct/incompetence; disclosing concealment of above. 2) There is a public interest in freedom of expression itself. 3) Regulator will consider extent material is already in public domain or will become so. 4) Editors must explain how they reasonably reached decision that publication served and was proportionate to public interest at the time. 5) Exceptional public interest required to over-ride normally paramount interests of children under 16.
